content: Heated and humidified air has traditionally been used as a remedy for the common cold. The underlying theory is that steam may facilitate the drainage of congested mucus and that heat might inactivate the cold virus, as observed in laboratory settings. This review is an update of a previous analysis published in 2013. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of inhaling heated water vapor (steam) on the treatment of the common cold. Specifically, the review aimed to compare symptom relief, viral shedding, and nasal resistance between those treated with heated, humidified air and control groups. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and Current Contents, covering studies up to February 2017. Additional searches were performed on the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov in March 2017. Reference lists of included studies were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials that investigated the use of heated water vapor in participants with naturally occurring or experimentally induced common colds. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed. Three authors independently screened studies for inclusion, and disagreements were resolved by a third author. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, and analyses were conducted using Review Manager 5 software. The review included six trials from five publications, involving a total of 387 participants. No new studies were added in this 2017 update. The risk of bias assessment indicated an unclear risk in the randomization process but a low risk in other domains, such as performance, detection, attrition, and reporting. The evidence regarding the effectiveness of heated, humidified air for symptom relief in the common cold was inconclusive. A fixed-effect analysis suggested a potential benefit (odds ratio [OR] 0.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.16 to 0.56; 2 studies, 149 participants). However, a random-effects analysis showed no statistically significant difference (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.95). Both forms of analysis have their merits, but the results were inconsistent. No studies reported a worsening of clinical symptom scores. One study conducted in the United States found that nasal resistance worsened with treatment, while an earlier study from Israel reported an improvement. Regarding viral shedding, one study found no significant difference between the treatment and placebo groups (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.04 to 5.19). Subjective responses to therapy, such as participants reporting that the treatment did not help, also showed no significant difference between groups (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.18; 2 studies, 124 participants). There was considerable variability in the effects of heated, humidified air on different outcomes, leading to the evidence being graded as low quality. Some studies reported minor adverse events, such as nasal discomfort or irritation. In conclusion, the current evidence does not demonstrate clear benefits or harms associated with the use of heated, humidified air, such as that delivered via the RhinoTherm device, for treating the common cold. Further research is needed, particularly double-blind, randomized trials with standardized treatment protocols, to clarify the potential role of this intervention.
